content: The implementation of two rounds of mass drug administration (MDA) targeting all at-risk groups with adequate treatment coverage (defined as ≥75%) is recommended. The relative reduction in disease prevalence can be calculated using the formula: [(prevalence at baseline prevalence at year 3) / (prevalence at baseline)]. However, the scientific basis for this threshold is still evolving, and the definition is considered provisional. It is provided to encourage standardization in reporting. Preschool-aged children are defined as those between 24 and 59 months of age who are typically not yet attending primary school. The prevalence of infection refers to the percentage of individuals of all ages in a population targeted for treatment who are infected with any species of Schistosoma. Preventive chemotherapy involves the large-scale administration of medicines, either alone or in combination, as part of public health interventions. Mass drug administration (MDA) is one form of preventive chemotherapy, while other forms may target specific population groups, such as school-aged children or women of childbearing age. In this context, preventive chemotherapy refers to the large-scale use of anthelmintic medicines in specific population groups, as opposed to MDA for the entire population. School-aged children are generally defined as those between 5 and 15 years of age, regardless of whether they are attending school. However, the exact ages for school enrollment may vary between countries, and in some cases, primary school enrollment may include individuals older than 15 years. Treatment coverage is defined as the proportion of individuals in a defined population who received the treatment. The defined population may include (i) a target group for treatment, such as school-aged children; (ii) the entire population of a geographical region, administrative area, or community where specific diseases are highly endemic; or (iii) the entire population of a country. These types of coverage are referred to as (i) programmatic coverage, (ii) geographical coverage, and (iii) national coverage, respectively. Adequate treatment coverage for schistosomiasis is defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as treating ≥75% of the target population. Human schistosomiasis is a chronic parasitic disease caused by infection with blood flukes (trematode worms) of the genus Schistosoma. It is a significant public health problem in tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and South America. Approximately 779 million people are at risk of acquiring the infection, and 6 million people required preventive chemotherapy in 2019. Schistosomiasis is classified as a neglected tropical disease (NTD), a group of diseases that predominantly affect low-income populations worldwide. In response to resolutions adopted by the World Health Assembly and in alignment with WHO’s 13th General Programme of Work (2019–2023), WHO supports member states in expanding access to prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care interventions for NTDs to contribute to achieving universal health coverage by 2030. In 2020, WHO published a new roadmap to guide action against NTDs during the decade 2021–2030. The roadmap aims to eliminate schistosomiasis as a public health problem by 2030 and to interrupt schistosome transmission in humans in selected countries by 2030. Achieving these targets will contribute to progress toward Sustainable Development Goal 3: “Ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages.” WHO’s strategy to control and eliminate human schistosomiasis includes preventive chemotherapy for at-risk groups, access to improved drinking water, improved sanitation, hygiene education, environmental management, and snail control. This WHO guideline was developed in accordance with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2014). A guideline steering group was established to formulate key questions using the Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome (PICO) format and to prioritize outcomes. The PICO questions were reviewed by a guideline development group (GDG) and used to systematically retrieve, appraise, and synthesize evidence, formulate recommendations, and plan for dissemination and implementation. All policy recommendations were formulated through consensus based on the GDG’s judgments, informed by evidence and the expertise and experience of its members. In cases where consensus was not reached, a voting process was adopted. An external review group provided comments on the final draft of the guideline but could not alter the recommendations made by the GDG. The goal of this guideline is to provide evidence-based recommendations to countries in their efforts to achieve schistosomiasis morbidity control and elimination as a public health problem and to move toward interrupting transmission. The recommendations aim to help countries implement national schistosomiasis control and elimination programs and support efforts to verify the interruption of transmission. Specific objectives include providing guidance on prevalence thresholds, target age groups, and the frequency of preventive chemotherapy; establishing water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and snail control activities; using diagnostic tests in low-transmission areas; assessing Schistosoma spp. infection in snail hosts; and diagnosing schistosomiasis in animal reservoirs. This guideline updates and supersedes previous schistosomiasis-related recommendations contained in several WHO publications, including the 2013 strategic plan, the 2006 manual for health professionals, and earlier technical reports. The rationale for developing this guideline includes the need for updated guidance based on evidence rather than expert opinion, the absence of previous guidance on evaluating the interruption of schistosomiasis transmission, and the continued public health significance of schistosomiasis in many countries. Preventive chemotherapy has demonstrated benefits but remains inaccessible to all affected communities. By providing a revised guideline, the aim is to empower health ministries and local communities to expand the use of preventive chemotherapy to support broader target populations in their efforts to control and eliminate the disease. From a patient and public health perspective, there is no acceptable level of schistosomiasis morbidity. The approaches recommended in this revised guideline are designed to eliminate morbidity from schistosomiasis, but sustained effort will be required. Recent impact assessment surveys have shown that the prevalence of schistosomiasis infection, as determined using parasitological techniques, has dropped to low levels in some countries. New guidance is therefore required for countries transitioning from morbidity control to elimination as a public health problem. Sensitive diagnostic tools have been developed for use in humans, animals, and snail intermediate hosts, and guidance is needed for their use, particularly in low-transmission areas. The key audiences for this guideline include policymakers, national NTD control programs, and task forces in health ministries, regional program review groups, and implementation partners. It is intended as a reference document for all stakeholders, including WHO, pharmaceutical manufacturers, donor organizations, nongovernmental organizations, and academic institutions. The guideline aims to empower and impact various groups, including residents of endemic communities, visitors to endemic areas, medicine distributors, program managers, and national regulatory authorities. This guideline is based on the best evidence available to the GDG in 2021. However, for many questions, the evidence base was limited and is subject to change. The guideline will be updated as new evidence emerges.
